ZETA

Zeta Global: the quarter that did everything at once

Marketing software that uses customer data and AI to decide who to contact, when and how.

Revenue rose 46% to $493 million. Excluding an acquisition (Marigold) and US election spending, underlying growth was 30%, up from 28% last quarter. Zeta also made a profit under the standard accounting rules, turned more of it into cash, and raised its forecasts for revenue, profit and cash for the 21st quarter in a row.

The main point

Growing fast and profitable at the same time

Software investors often use the "Rule of 40": add the revenue growth rate to the profit margin, and a total above 40 is seen as healthy. Fast growth usually costs profit, and high profit usually means slower growth. Zeta scored 71.

Profit margin here is adjusted EBITDA as a share of revenue.

What changed

Forecasts raised, and analysts behind

Zeta raised every number it guides on. The clearest sign of how far expectations have moved is its own forecast for GAAP earnings per share, which has risen nearly eightfold since January.

2026 guidance, midpointNewChange
Q4 revenue$523m+$15m. Analysts expected $510.4m

Under the radar

The points that did not make the headlines
  • Google search is changing, and Zeta says budgets are following. The chief executive said his understanding is that up to 68% of Google queries are now answered by Gemini, Google's AI, and that the share of searches ending in a click has fallen from over 90% to about 32%. Fewer clicks make search advertising more expensive, and he said "meaningful budget" is moving from search to Zeta.
  • Athena is the engine. Athena is Zeta's AI assistant for marketers. Over half of its largest customers now use it monthly, up from just over 40% last quarter. Customers using Athena make up about 70% of revenue, and the top 25 users grew their spend by more than 70%.
  • Demand is building. Requests for proposals more than doubled on a year ago. Its October customer event, Zeta Live, produced over $100m of pipeline and 23 signed deals so far.
  • Fewer new shares. Share-based pay has fallen from 33% of revenue in 2023 to 12% this year. Zeta has also bought back $101m of its own shares in 2026, with $63m left on the current plan.
  • AI is writing its own code. About 90% of new code is now generated automatically, which the company says has cut the time from idea to release by 27%.

What the market heard

Reaction and commentary

Shares slipped about 3% after hours, according to one early report. After 21 beats in a row, a beat is what the price already assumed. The shares were also up about 59% in 2026 before the results, the only one of the four in positive territory, so the bar was high.

Independent analysts on social media focused on two things: the consistency of the beats, and the Google comments, which several saw as the most under-discussed point of the call.

"We're starting to see meaningful budget move to Zeta from what was in search originally."

David Steinberg, chief executive, on the earnings call

The case for and against

Equal weight to both sides

The case for

  • Growth is speeding up while margins widen, a rare combination.
  • Real cash generation pays for buybacks and new products.
  • The biggest customers are growing in number and spend.
  • A possible long-term shift of budget away from search advertising.

The case against

  • After 21 beats, the market expects a beat. Merely meeting forecasts could hurt.
  • AthenaOS, the next product, is still in early testing.
  • The business depends on consumer data, where privacy rules keep tightening.
  • Part of 2026 growth came from an acquisition and election spending that will not repeat.

What to watch

The next few quarters
Athena
Whether usage keeps rising and lifts spend into 2027.
Pipeline
How much of the Zeta Live pipeline turns into signed revenue.
Margins
Whether margins hold as election revenue drops away.
AthenaOS
Release, expected by the end of Q1 2027, and early uptake.
The thesisTEI matrix: Working

The case rests on Zeta taking a growing share of marketing budgets as AI changes how brands find customers. Unlike the others, this is already showing in profit and cash. The question now is durability: can it keep beating while the bar keeps rising?

The TEI Growth Portfolio and the founder hold Zeta Global shares.

RKLB

Rocket Lab: a record quarter, overshadowed by one date

Builds satellites and satellite parts, and launches small rockets. Developing Neutron, a larger reusable rocket.

Revenue rose 73% to $268 million, the sixth record quarter in a row, with yearly revenue now running above $1 billion before Neutron has earned anything. Orders flooded in. But Neutron's first flight slipped to "no earlier than 2027" after a fault in a fuel tank part, and losses widened, so the shares fell after hours.

The main point

Demand is not the problem. Timing is.

Rocket Lab signed about $1 billion of launch contracts in one quarter. That included eight Neutron launches worth around $515 million, several at a new, higher base price of $70 million. All 16 of Neutron's first flights are now booked before it has flown once, and the next free slots are in the 2030s.

The company said it could have booked more, but chose a higher price over more volume, because it expects launch prices to keep rising.

The numbers

Results, segments and backlog
MeasureQ3 2026ChangeWhat it tells us

Space Systems$214.8m+13% on Q2Satellites and parts, now four fifths of revenue.
Launch$53.1m+19% on Q2Two more Electron launches than last quarter.
Gross margin33.6%down on Q2Above guidance. Pulled down by a recent laser communications purchase.

Cash and investments$4.7bnBoosted by selling $2.4bn of new shares.

What changed

Neutron, guidance and the path to profit
  • Neutron moves to 2027 at the earliest. A defect was found in the forward dome of the first-stage tank. A replacement is ready but must pass its tests. The chief executive declined to give a month or quarter, saying he did not want to be "continually wrong".
  • Fourth-quarter guidance. Revenue of $270m to $290m and gross margin improving to 34% to 36%. Adjusted EBITDA loss of $14m to $20m.
  • The route to profit. Management said adjusted EBITDA should turn positive within about six months of a successful first Neutron flight, with cash flow following later as Neutron moves into production.
  • Iridium. The purchase of Iridium, a satellite phone network, is fully funded and approved by Iridium shareholders. It still needs regulators and is expected to close in 2027.

Under the radar

The points that did not make the headlines
  • A US government loan for Neutron. The Department of War's Office of Strategic Capital announced a $150m conditional loan commitment to help Rocket Lab build more Neutrons, add recovery ships and turn rockets around faster. Conditions must be met before it is final. Management estimated the interest rate at about 1 point above the benchmark rate.
  • Data centres in space. The chief executive said smaller data centres in orbit are "completely doable" for defence use: "It's pretty hard to tamper with something when it's in orbit." Rocket Lab makes solar cells for spacecraft, and Iridium would add secure communications, so it could supply both.
  • Space Systems orders. $470m of new Space Systems contracts in the quarter, five times the same quarter last year.
  • Factory pace. An Electron rocket now leaves the production line every eight working days on average. Twelve Rocket Lab-built spacecraft launched in the past year, with more than 55 in build.
  • Biggest orders ever. 18 HASTE launches for the US Space Force and 20 Electron launches for Synspective, a Japanese satellite company.

What the market heard

Reaction and commentary

The shares had risen about 25% in the two days before the results and closed up 11% at $58.86 on the day. A record quarter was already in the price. The Neutron delay was the new information, and the shares fell between 4% and 8% after hours and overnight. They are down about 16% in 2026 and well below their high of $151, set on 27 May.

One US analyst argued the delay matters less than it looks, pointing to Rocket Lab's position in spacecraft solar cells and, through Iridium, in secure communications. The more cautious reading focused on the cost of waiting for Neutron and the new shares issued this year.

The case for and against

Equal weight to both sides

The case for

  • Demand is bigger than supply. Customers are paying more and booking years ahead.
  • Space Systems is now the larger, steadier business.
  • $4.7bn of cash and government support for Neutron.
  • Iridium would add recurring revenue and cash flow.

The case against

  • Neutron has slipped more than once. A failed first flight would push everything back again.
  • Losses are widening while Neutron is built.
  • 36.8m new shares sold this year, with more dilution possible.
  • Iridium adds debt and integration risk.

What to watch

The next few quarters
Neutron
Tank tests, then a firm first-flight date.
Q4 delivery
Revenue of $270m to $290m and the promised margin rise.
Iridium
Regulatory approval and closing in 2027.
Dilution
Further share sales or debt to fund growth.
The thesisTEI matrix: Patience

The case rests on Rocket Lab becoming the main alternative to SpaceX: launch, spacecraft and, with Iridium, services in orbit. Space Systems already pays the bills. Neutron is what turns it into a much larger business, and its first flight date is the variable that matters most.

TEI does not hold Rocket Lab shares. The Growth Portfolio's space exposure already comes through AST SpaceMobile, so adding it would mean replacing another holding or concentrating further in one sector.

ASTS

AST SpaceMobile: judged on satellites, not on revenue

Building a network of large satellites, called BlueBirds, that connect directly to ordinary mobile phones.

Revenue nearly tripled to $42.3 million but came in below forecasts, and the loss was $0.44 a share. For a company still building its network, the numbers that matter are when the service switches on, how many satellites reach orbit, and how long the cash lasts. On all three there was news.

$400m to $500m

The main point

From "can they build it?" to "can they switch it on?"

AST expects to start intermittent, nationwide phone service before the end of 2026 in the US, Canada, Japan, Saudi Arabia and the UK, using the satellites already in orbit. "Intermittent" means coverage comes and goes as satellites pass over.

Continuous service needs roughly 45 to 60 satellites. The plan is about 45 in orbit by mid-2027 and over 100 under launch contracts by the end of 2028.

The numbers

Revenue, spending and cash
MeasureQ3 2026ChangeWhat it tells us
Revenue$42.3mnearly 3xGround equipment sales and US government milestones. No meaningful recurring phone service revenue yet.
Adjusted operating costs$133.6mfrom $119.1mMore staff and bigger factories. Q4 expected higher again.
Capital spendingabout $310mfrom $610mBelow plan only because launch payments moved into Q4.
Net loss to shareholders$132.4mfrom $122.9m-$0.44 a share.
Cash$3.2bnIncludes $1.15bn raised through convertible bonds in July.
2026 revenue guidance$150m to $200mheldNeeds a much larger fourth quarter. Management said it has "high confidence".

What changed

A rocket, a Japanese deal and a faster chip
  • Its own rocket, Blacklift. A 20-tonne reusable rocket using engine technology licensed from Firefly Aerospace, able to carry up to five BlueBirds at a time. First launches are expected in late 2028. It is meant to sit alongside SpaceX and Blue Origin, not replace them. More detail is due at an event on Thursday 12 November.
  • Japan. A joint venture with Rakuten, 49% owned by AST, is set to receive about $1 billion of Japanese government grants over roughly three years, mostly in 2027, to build and launch satellites for Japan. This "non-dilutive" money funds growth without new shares. The news lifted the shares 14% during Monday's session.
  • A better chip, sooner. A new processor giving 10 times the processing power of the first BlueBirds has been brought forward to satellite 34, from satellite 50. Production is targeted at six satellites a month from December.

Under the radar

The points that did not make the headlines
  • A first with AT&T. AST and AT&T moved a phone connection between a ground mast and a satellite without dropping it, which the company says is a first. That matters because users would not notice the switch.
  • Reach, not revenue. AST works with over 60 mobile networks covering more than 3 billion subscribers. These are potential customers through partners, not paying users yet.
  • Government work. 16 US government awards so far, including a Space Force contract worth about $100m for space-based sensing.
  • More funding lined up. Management pointed to a further $1.2bn of possible non-dilutive US government-linked financing in 2027.
  • Legal risk. A shareholder class action was filed in September 2026, alleging misleading statements between March 2025 and July 2026. AST's convertible bonds could also add about 40 million shares if converted.

What the market heard

Reaction and commentary

The shares rose 14% to $36.89 on Monday on the Rakuten news, before the results. After hours they were little changed. Even after Monday's jump, the shares are down about 49% in 2026.

Before the results, options prices implied a move of about 22% either way. The move after the results was close to nothing, a sign that the Rakuten news had already done the work and the quarterly numbers changed little.

The case for and against

Equal weight to both sides

The case for

  • Partnerships with major networks give a route to billions of phones.
  • Grant money funds part of the build without new shares.
  • Technical firsts, like the AT&T handover, are being proven.
  • A second customer type in the US government.

The case against

  • Revenue is tiny against spending, and any launch delay pushes it back.
  • Building a rocket adds a second large engineering project.
  • Convertible bonds and the class action add risk for shareholders.
  • Rivals, including SpaceX, already offer phone-to-satellite services.

What to watch

The next few quarters
Service
Intermittent service actually switching on by year end.
Launches
BlueBirds 14 to 25 reaching orbit on schedule.
Q4 revenue
Enough to reach at least the $150m low end.
Blacklift
Cost and funding detail at the 12 November event.
The thesisTEI matrix: Patience

The case rests on the business AST can become, not the one it reports today. Once the constellation is built and phone service is live through mobile networks around the world, it would earn recurring revenue on a very large base of subscribers. For now, the quarterly numbers say little. Continuous coverage needs about 45 to 60 satellites, which the company expects to start reaching from mid-2027. That is when the numbers can start to show, and when they matter.

The TEI Growth Portfolio and the founder hold AST SpaceMobile shares.

HIMS

Hims & Hers: growing fast while changing what it sells

An online health platform. Customers subscribe for treatments prescribed through the app.

Revenue grew 49% to $890 million, the second quarter in a row of faster growth. But Hims & Hers is moving its weight-loss business from cheaper compounded drugs to branded drugs from Novo Nordisk and Eli Lilly. Branded drugs bring in more revenue per customer, but the company keeps less of each dollar. The result was a surprise loss, fewer subscribers and a lower profit forecast.

The main point

More revenue, less kept from each dollar

Gross margin fell 17 points in a year. That is the cost of selling branded weight-loss drugs, which cost the company more to buy, and of expanding abroad.

Management called it a deliberate trade: broader choice now, for stronger growth later. The market will want to see the margin settle before believing it.

What changed

Guidance, Lilly and the subscriber dip
  • Profit forecast cut. 2026 adjusted EBITDA is now expected at $257m to $277m. The revenue range was narrowed to $3.13bn to $3.15bn, from $3.1bn to $3.3bn. Fourth-quarter revenue is expected at $875m to $895m.
  • Fewer subscribers, on purpose. Subscribers fell from 2.89m to 2.79m, against an analyst forecast of 3.04m. Management said it held back US weight-loss marketing until Lilly's drugs join the platform, and warned of one more weak subscriber quarter before growth returns.
  • Lilly joins Novo. A new agreement with Eli Lilly brings Zepbound and Foundayo to the platform, alongside Novo Nordisk's Wegovy pen and pill. The aim is a full range of weight-loss options by early 2027.
  • International raised. International revenue is now expected to pass $650m in 2026, up from $600m, with a $1bn yearly run-rate targeted for 2027.

Under the radar

The points that did not make the headlines
  • The Huberman deal. Andrew Huberman, the neuroscientist and podcaster, joined the board on 4 November. He also has paid advisory and advertising agreements, so the board does not count him as independent. The potential cost is about $24m over three years, before his board fees.
  • Hers is nearly a $1bn business. The women's brand is heading for about $1bn of revenue this year, helped by dermatology and menopause care.
  • Testosterone. Approaching a $100m yearly run-rate, with injectable treatments added last month.
  • Peptides. A Peptides+ offering is due later in November after US rules were eased, though the company says it will scale carefully while regulation settles.
  • AI care. An AI-led experience reached 70% of weight-loss subscribers and is expected to reach nearly all of them by year end.

What the market heard

Reaction and commentary

The shares fell 12% during Monday's session and a further 3% after hours. The loss and the lower profit forecast outweighed the revenue growth. They are down about 29% in 2026.

Independent analysts on social media were split on Huberman: some saw high-value access to a large, trusting audience, others an expensive bet while margins are falling. A fund manager who owns the shares told Reuters that "margin compression was to be expected".

The case for and against

Equal weight to both sides

The case for

  • Revenue growth is speeding up, not slowing.
  • Revenue per subscriber up 30%.
  • Offering both Novo and Lilly drugs widens choice.
  • Still cash positive with $710m in the bank.

The case against

  • Margins down sharply and the profit forecast cut.
  • Losing subscribers while revenue grows can hide weaker demand.
  • Telehealth, compounding and peptides face changing rules.
  • Large commitments to Huberman during a margin squeeze.

What to watch

The next few quarters
Subscribers
Whether growth returns in Q1 2027 as promised.
Gross margin
Whether it stops falling as the product mix settles.
Lilly
How quickly Zepbound and Foundayo add customers.
Huberman
Any visible lift in sign-ups for newer categories.
The thesisTEI matrix: between Patience and Watching

The case rests on distribution. Hims & Hers has built a direct, paying relationship with nearly 2.8 million subscribers, and the long-term idea is a "Netflix of healthcare": one subscription, many treatments, across many countries. Weight loss brings customers in. This quarter the evidence moved the wrong way, with margins down and subscribers falling. We still have conviction in the idea, but it needs to prove itself, so it sits on the line between Patience and Watching. Margins settling and subscriber growth returning in early 2027 would move it back towards Patience.

TEI does not hold Hims & Hers shares.

What this does not say

  • It does not say whether any of these shares is worth buying, holding or selling. That depends on personal circumstances, goals and how much risk is right, which is outside the scope of this article.
  • It does not give a price target or forecast. Guidance figures are the companies' own, analysts' forecasts are third-party estimates, and both can change.
  • One quarter is a short window. A delayed launch, a cut forecast or a strong beat can look very different a year later.
  • After-hours prices come from thin, early trading and often reverse by the next close.
  • Comments from management, such as Zeta's figures on Google search, are their view and have not been independently checked.
  • What would change the picture: a successful or failed first Neutron flight, the pace of BlueBird launches and the service switch-on, Hims & Hers subscriber numbers in early 2027, and whether Zeta's new AI products turn into revenue.

Glossary
Consensus
The average forecast of the analysts who follow a company. A "beat" or "miss" is measured against it.
GAAP
The standard US accounting rules. "Adjusted" or "non-GAAP" figures strip out some costs the company sees as one-off or non-cash.
Net income
Profit under the accounting rules, after every cost, including ones not paid in cash.
Free cash flow
The cash left after running the business and paying for equipment and software.
Adjusted EBITDA
Earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, with some other costs removed. A rough measure of operating profit.
Gross margin
The share of revenue left after the direct cost of what was sold.
Backlog
Signed contracts not yet delivered, so not yet counted as revenue.
Guidance
A company's own forecast for the coming quarter or year.
Dilution
When new shares are issued, each existing share owns a smaller slice of the company.
Convertible bond
A loan the lender can swap for shares at a set price. Cheap borrowing now, possible dilution later.
